title: Comparative Genomics and Cold-Stress Transcriptomic Responses of Yeasts from Antarctic and Andean Environments
content: Microorganisms inhabiting cold environments face multiple stressors, particularly low and freezing temperatures, that drive diverse molecular and metabolic responses. Cold-adapted yeasts are ecologically important and hold biotechnological potential; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying their responses to cold remain comparatively understudied. In this study, we compared nuclear and putative mitochondrial genomes, along with transcriptional responses to cold stress, in four yeast isolates: two identified as Rhodotorula mucilaginosa, one from Antarctica and the other from the central Chilean Andes, and Antarctic isolates of Sporobolomyces salmonicolor and Vishniacozyma victoriae. The two R. mucilaginosa isolates exhibited extensive genomic synteny conservation and broad functional similarities, whereas the V. victoriae isolate showed a distinct genomic profile. Mitochondrial genome assemblies varied in size (20.8–58.1 kb), gene content, and intron abundance. Cold exposure moderately affected growth rates but markedly reduced final biomass across the isolates. Although the isolates exhibited distinct global transcriptional profiles at their respective optimal growth temperatures, the two R. mucilaginosa isolates showed greater transcriptional similarity under cold stress. Furthermore, we identified pathways associated with cold exposure, some of which returned toward their initial expression patterns during recovery, whereas others remained altered into the stationary phase. Overall, our findings indicate that cold exposure elicits both transient transcriptional responses and sustained changes in gene expression in yeasts from cold environments. They also suggest that transcriptional responses to cold may be more closely associated with taxonomic identity than with geographic origin.
